newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China not seen active in vegetable oil market.
newsitem.headline: China not seen active in vegetable oil market.

text.p: An extended National Day holiday and a lack of official import licences are keeping China out of the soybean oil market, Far East grain and oil seed traders said on Wednesday.
"There are no licences," a Singapore source said. "It's not a question of price, it's a question of quota and no one has it."
Beijing usually issues quotas for vegetable oil imports around mid-year but has yet to announce them for 1996.
Many traders doubt licences have been issued, though one Hong Kong trading source says licences for 300,000 tonnes of vegetable oil other than palm have been granted.
However, a good rapeseed crop of around eight million tonnes meant that imports were not yet viable, he said.
Soy oil imported without a licence carries a 120 percent import tax; importers with licences must pay 13 percent import duty and a 13 percent value-added tax on top of that, traders said.
Soyoil futures prices rose on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) on Tuesday amid talk China was seeking four or five cargoes of soybean oil.
By midday, soyoil was 0.03 to 0.12 cent per lb higher, with October up 0.09 at 23.95 cents per lb.
By CBOT's close, U.S. exporters had discounted the China talk after confirmation Morroco had bought the vegetable oil for November/December delivery.
China's October 1 National Day saw markets and business close down until Wednesday, with traders expecting things to remain slow for the rest of the week.
"China has been on holiday for the past two days, so there have been no inquiries," a European trader in Hong Kong said.
"There have been some freight inquiries, but that is optional destination," he said. "This is what I will be keeping my eye on."
